segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I want you to know how great a struggle I have for you and for those in Laodicea, and for all who have not seen my face in the flesh,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: that their hearts may be encouraged, as they are knit together in love and come into all the wealth of the full assurance that understanding brings, into the knowledge of God’s mystery, Christ,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I say this so that no one may deceive you with plausible-sounding arguments.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For even if I am absent in the flesh, I am still with you in spirit, rejoicing to see your good order and the firmness of your faith in Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, walk in him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: rooted and being built up in him and made firm in the faith, just as you were taught, overflowing with thanksgiving.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: See to it that no one carries you off as plunder through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For in him all the fullness of deity dwells bodily,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and you have been made full in him, who is the head of every ruler and authority.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In him you were also circumcised with a circumcision not made by hands, in the stripping off of the body of flesh, in the circumcision of Christ,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: having been buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him through faith in the working of God, who raised him from the dead.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And when you were dead in your trespasses and the uncircumcision of your flesh, God made you alive together with him. He forgave us all our trespasses,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: erasing the record of debt that stood against us with its decrees and was hostile to us; he has taken it out of the way, nailing it to the cross.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He stripped the rulers and the authorities and made a public show of them, leading them in triumphal procession in him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So do not let anyone judge you over what you eat or drink, or in the matter of a festival, a new moon, or a sabbath.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: These are a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Let no one who delights in self-abasement and the worship of angels disqualify you, going on in detail about what he has seen, puffed up without cause by his fleshly mind,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and not holding fast to the head, from whom the whole body, nourished and knit together through its joints and ligaments, grows with the growth that comes from God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If you died with Christ to the elements of the world, why, as though still living in the world, do you submit to decrees:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Do not handle, do not taste, do not touch,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: which all concern things destined to perish with use, according to human commands and teachings?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Such things do have a reputation for wisdom, with their self-chosen worship and self-abasement and severity to the body, but they are of no value against the gratification of the flesh.

notes.traditional: the mystery of God, and of the Father, and of Christ
notes.note: The manuscripts give this phrase in many different forms, including the longer one behind the King James Version. Most textual critics judge the short and abrupt 'of the mystery of God, Christ' to be original, with the other forms as scribal attempts to smooth it. 'Christ' is most naturally read as explaining what the mystery is, as translated; 'the mystery of the God of Christ' is grammatically possible but unlikely.

In the first century 'philosophy' covered any organized body of teaching with its way of life, religious as well as intellectual, and Jewish writers used the word of Judaism and its schools. A single Greek article joins 'philosophy' and 'empty deceit', so one thing is in view. It is a particular teaching on offer at Colossae, not the discipline of philosophy as such.

notes.traditional: rudiments of the world (KJV); elemental spirits (RSV, NRSV, ESV); elementary principles (NASB)
notes.note: The Greek word means the basic components of something: letters of the alphabet, first principles of a subject, or the physical elements. In writers of the period the full phrase 'elements of the world' regularly means the physical elements (earth, water, air, fire) of which the world was thought to be made, and that plain rendering is kept here. Many scholars instead understand spiritual powers believed to govern the cosmos, a sense not clearly attested for the word until later, and others understand 'elementary teachings'. The question is unresolved; the phrase recurs in verse 20.

This can mean a circumcision that Christ performs or that belongs to him, in contrast to the physical rite. It can also be a metaphor for Christ's own death, in which his 'body of flesh' was stripped away. On the first reading 'the body of flesh' is the believer's old self; on the second it is Christ's physical body. The translation leaves both open, as the Greek does.

The Greek pronoun can also be read 'in whom', continuing the series of 'in him' phrases that runs through verses 6 to 11. Most translations take it of baptism, as here, since baptism is the nearest noun and burial and rising form a natural pair.

The Greek word means a handwritten document, and in everyday use a note of debt written in the debtor's own hand. Ink of the period could be washed or wiped off, which is the picture behind 'erasing'. How the 'decrees' relate to the document, whether as its terms or as the grounds of the debt, is debated.

The verb is the counterpart of the noun 'stripping off' in verse 11 and literally refers to taking off clothing. Most modern translations read 'disarmed', with God stripping the powers of their weapons or dignity. Many early Greek interpreters instead took it as 'stripped off from himself', with Christ shedding the powers at the cross. 'Stripped' keeps the echo of verse 11 and suits the picture of captives displayed in a triumph.

notes.phrase: leading them in triumphal procession in him
notes.note: The verb refers to the Roman triumph, in which a victorious general paraded defeated enemies through the city as a public humiliation. 'The rulers and the authorities' here are spiritual powers, not human officials. The final phrase can equally be translated 'in it', meaning the cross; 'in him' assumes that God is still the subject, as in verse 13, and that the triumph takes place in Christ.

The Greek word is 'body', used here in a common contrast between a shadow and the solid thing that casts it. Because 'body' also means the church in this letter (verse 19), some hear a second sense: the reality is found in the body of Christ. Most translations render 'substance' or 'reality', as here.

This is the ordinary word for humility, which is elsewhere a virtue. Here and in verse 23 it names something the rival teachers insist on and take pride in, apparently a practice: in Jewish and early Christian usage 'humbling oneself' often referred to fasting and similar rigors. 'Self-abasement' marks that sense; several modern versions use it or 'asceticism', while others keep 'humility' or 'false humility'.

This is usually understood as worship offered to angels. The Greek can equally mean the worship that angels themselves offer, in which case the teachers claimed to witness or join the heavenly worship in visions, an idea found in Jewish texts of the period. Scholarship is divided.

notes.phrase: going on in detail about what he has seen
notes.traditional: intruding into those things which he hath not seen
notes.note: This is one of the most obscure phrases in the letter. The verb basically means to enter or set foot on, and can mean to go into a subject in detail. It also appears in later inscriptions for entering a sanctuary after initiation, so 'which he saw on entering', of a visionary experience, is also possible. Later manuscripts add 'not' ('what he has not seen'), which lies behind the King James rendering; the earliest witnesses lack it.

notes.phrase: of no value against the gratification of the flesh
notes.traditional: not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh
notes.note: The Greek of this verse is compressed and its syntax is disputed. The rendering here, that such rules have no value in restraining self-indulgence, is the majority view. The words can also be taken to mean that the rules are of no value and serve only to gratify the flesh, that is, the pride of the one who keeps them.

candidates.reason: The phrase 'elements of the world' recurs in Galatians 4 and the word in Hebrews 5 and 2 Peter 3; translations split between 'elements', 'elemental spirits' and 'elementary principles', and readers would be confused by variation.
It recurs across the Gospels, Paul and Revelation, and 'mystery' suggests a puzzle where the Greek means a secret now disclosed, so one policy ('mystery' or 'secret') is needed.
It is used here for physical presence, the physical body and the sinful self within a single chapter, and translations vary widely between 'flesh', 'body', 'sinful nature' and paraphrase.
The Semitic idiom of 'walking' for conducting one's life recurs throughout the letters, and translators divide between 'walk' and 'live'.

It recurs in Paul and the Gospels; 'trespass' now chiefly suggests entering property, and alternatives such as 'offense', 'transgression' and 'sin' overlap with other Greek words that need to be kept distinct.
